strengths: The paper addresses a well-defined and underexplored problem: optimal binary post-processing under sufficiency/predictive parity for finite-valued calibrated scores. The finite-score setting is practically important and avoids the continuity/full-support assumptions of prior work.

The main geometric formulation in terms of feasible PPV/FOR pairs is elegant. The star-convexity argument, the fractional-knapsack characterization of the boundary, and the reduction of group sufficiency to intersections of group feasible regions provide useful conceptual understanding.

The proposed boundary-tracing framework gives constructive algorithms for optimizing broad objectives under sufficiency, including loss minimization and minimizing deviation from separation. The appendices provide many derivations and make the theoretical development reasonably checkable.
The COMPAS example illustrates that the framework can be applied to discrete real-world scores and that sufficient classifiers may require group-specific randomized or threshold-like rules.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is very limited. The only real-data experiment is a single COMPAS example with one random calibration/distribution split, no uncertainty estimates, no comparison to Baumann et al. or Canetti et al. implementations, no runtime/scaling study, and no sensitivity analysis to calibration error. This makes the practical claims, such as performance being often comparable to the optimum, weakly supported.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper provides algorithms and formulas but no code, no exact preprocessing details for COMPAS beyond a high-level split, no random seed, no sample counts after filtering, and no precise calibration values or score distributions. A reader could reimplement the method, but reproducing Figure 3 and the reported accuracies would be difficult.

Some claims are stated too strongly or imprecisely. In Section 4.1, the text says that membership in C0 intersection C1 is equivalent to the global bounds in Eq. 9, but those bounds are only necessary without also enforcing the subgroup boundary constraints; the later boundary-max construction effectively uses the missing constraints. This does not obviously invalidate the method, but it signals a presentation/soundness gap that should be corrected.

The scope is narrower than some wording suggests: binary protected attribute in the main text, finite calibrated scores, known group-conditional score distributions, and exact group calibration. The extension to arbitrary finite groups is asserted as straightforward but not developed, and calibration error/statistical estimation error are not analyzed.

The paper lacks a substantive limitations and ethics discussion despite operating in high-stakes domains such as criminal justice, admissions, and lending. In particular, it does not discuss the normative concerns of using protected attributes at decision time, the instability of fairness guarantees under distribution shift, or harms from optimizing predictive parity alone.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional. The contribution is a useful finite-discrete geometric/post-processing treatment, but it builds closely on established fairness definitions, post-processing ideas, calibration/sufficiency tradeoffs, and knapsack-style threshold characterizations.

strengths: The paper targets a clear and relevant gap: post-processing finite-valued calibrated scores under sufficiency/predictive parity, where continuous-score assumptions in prior work are not directly applicable.

The geometric view of feasible PPV/FOR pairs is conceptually useful. The knapsack/soft-threshold characterization for a fixed selection rate is intuitive and could be a helpful tool for reasoning about randomized classifiers from discrete score bins.
The manuscript is mostly readable and self-contained, with proofs for many algebraic claims placed in appendices and a concrete COMPAS illustration that helps explain the intended use case.
weaknesses: The central theoretical development appears to contain a serious overstatement: Eq. (9) claims an iff characterization of membership in C0 intersect C1 using only rectangular bounds on p and q. Earlier results only establish necessary bounds; membership should also depend on the group-specific feasible-region boundary curves. This weakens confidence in later intersection and boundary arguments unless the missing sufficiency argument is supplied.

The paper assumes access to exactly group-calibrated finite scores and known group-wise score distributions, but the only real-data example estimates calibration from a small split without uncertainty analysis. The main claims are distributional/exact, yet practical deployment would operate under estimation error, miscalibration, and finite-sample noise, none of which are analyzed.

The empirical evaluation is far too thin for an ICML contribution: a single COMPAS use case, one random split, no confidence intervals, no ablations, no comparison to existing post-processing methods, and no evaluation of robustness to calibration error or sample size.

Reproducibility is weak. The paper does not provide code, exact processed score tables, random seeds, split details beyond 20/80 stratification, or enough numerical intermediate values to reproduce Figure 3 and the reported accuracies reliably.

The significance is limited by the narrow setting: binary groups, binary labels, finite calibrated scores, randomized post-processing, and largely population-level known distributions. The paper says extension to arbitrary finite groups is straightforward but does not spell out complexity, implementation, or failure modes.

The treatment of limitations and ethics is inadequate. There is no explicit limitations section, no discussion of harms from using protected attributes in post-processing, no discussion of whether sufficiency is normatively appropriate in settings such as COMPAS, and no analysis of how randomized decisions would be justified in high-stakes applications.

Presentation is polished at the local algebra level but underspecified at the contribution level: several algorithmic steps are pushed to appendices, formal correctness and complexity statements for the full algorithm are not highlighted clearly, and the relation to Baumann et al. and Canetti et al. is mostly qualitative rather than a precise comparison.

strengths: The paper studies a clean and practically relevant gap: enforcing sufficiency/predictive parity for finite-valued group-calibrated scores, where prior continuous/full-support assumptions are not appropriate for common score systems such as deciles.

The geometric characterization of attainable (PPV, FOR) pairs is elegant and useful. The reduction to a fractional knapsack/soft-threshold rule, the star-convex structure, and the piecewise boundary formula give a clear constructive understanding of the feasible set.

The extension to two groups via intersections of group-wise feasible regions is a natural but nontrivial step, and the boundary-tracing algorithm provides an exact post-processing route for optimizing losses under sufficiency.
The paper goes beyond loss minimization by considering deviation from separation under a sufficiency constraint, which helps clarify the tradeoff between incompatible fairness notions.
Presentation is mostly strong: definitions are clear, the figures support the geometric intuition, and the appendices provide detailed algebraic derivations.
weaknesses: There is a notable technical/presentation issue around Eq. (9): the stated 'iff' characterization of membership in C0 ∩ C1 using only rectangular bounds appears false. For each group, feasibility also requires q to lie above the group-specific lower boundary q_a(p), not merely above s_min. The later boundary construction uses max{q0(p), q1(p)}, so the algorithmic development may survive, but the statement as written is mathematically misleading and should be corrected.

The empirical evaluation is very limited. The COMPAS example is illustrative, but it uses a single random split, gives few dataset details or sample sizes, reports only one accuracy comparison, and does not provide uncertainty estimates, sensitivity to calibration split, or comparisons to relevant post-processing baselines.

Reproducibility is only partial. The theoretical algorithms are specified, but no implementation details, code, seed, or full calibrated score distributions are provided for the COMPAS experiment, making it hard to reproduce the numerical claims exactly.

The paper assumes exact group calibration of finite scores for the main theory. The COMPAS example explicitly estimates calibration empirically, but the paper does not analyze robustness to calibration error or finite-sample uncertainty, which is important because sufficiency constraints can be sensitive to estimation noise.

The scope is somewhat narrow: the main development is for binary groups in the body, with multi-group extension described as straightforward but not worked out. Since fairness applications often involve multiple or intersecting protected groups, this limits immediate applicability.

Ethical discussion is underdeveloped. The method explicitly uses protected group membership at decision time and can yield group-specific randomized rules; this may be legally or socially contested in some deployment settings and deserves a more explicit limitations and governance discussion.

strengths: The paper gives a clean and technically plausible geometric characterization of attainable (PPV, FOR) pairs for finite calibrated scores, then extends it to sufficiency by intersecting group-wise feasible regions.
The resulting post-processing algorithm is well motivated by the theory and supports exact optimization of several objectives, including 0-1 loss and a deviation-from-separation criterion.

The manuscript is clearly written, with useful figures, detailed appendices, and experiments on FICO, COMPAS, and ACS Income that illustrate when thresholding is insufficient and randomized post-processing is needed.

The authors acknowledge key limitations, especially reliance on group-calibrated scores, finite score supports, and the increasing restrictiveness of exact sufficiency with more groups; the robustness appendix usefully analyzes calibration error.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is mostly illustrative rather than deeply validating: FICO and COMPAS use aggregate or constructed score models, and COMPAS is treated as group-calibrated via pooled empirical decile rates despite only approximate sufficiency.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the paper states that code will be made available but provides no actual repository link, and some experimental details such as model hyperparameters and implementation choices are not sufficient for exact replication.

The main theory is developed for binary protected groups, with the multi-group extension described as straightforward but not fully developed; this matters because the conclusion itself notes feasibility becomes more restrictive with more groups.

The method depends on randomized, group-aware decision rules. The paper discusses fairness motivation but gives limited treatment of practical or ethical concerns around using protected attributes at decision time and deploying randomized decisions in high-stakes settings.

The contribution is useful and fairly original in the finite-score sufficiency setting, but its scope is specialized and builds closely on existing fairness post-processing and sufficiency literature, so the significance is moderate rather than broad.

strengths: The paper studies a clear and practically relevant fairness problem: converting calibrated finite-valued scores into binary decisions while enforcing sufficiency/predictive parity. This is a meaningful gap because ordinary thresholding can destroy sufficiency even when scores are calibrated.

The geometric characterization of feasible PPV/FOR pairs is elegant and appears technically coherent. The reduction to boundary tracing and fractional-knapsack-style soft thresholding gives a concrete algorithmic route rather than only an existence result.

The manuscript is unusually explicit about the finite-score setting, which is important for real scorecards such as FICO and COMPAS. It also acknowledges key limitations: dependence on group-calibrated scores, approximate calibration in practice, and the increasing restrictiveness of exact sufficiency with more groups.

The empirical examples are well chosen for the fairness setting and illustrate a nontrivial point: the optimal sufficient classifier often cannot be represented by deterministic thresholding in both groups.
weaknesses: The contribution is narrower than the abstract framing suggests. The core method assumes finite group-calibrated scores and binary protected groups in the main development; the extension to more groups is asserted as straightforward but not developed algorithmically or empirically. This limits significance for ICML unless the theoretical novelty over prior post-processing work is made sharper.

The empirical evaluation is mostly illustrative rather than convincing. FICO and COMPAS use aggregate or constructed score distributions and no learned model; COMPAS is explicitly treated as group-calibrated by assigning pooled empirical decile rates despite only approximate sufficiency. These choices weaken the evidential support for claims about practical deployment.

The ACS experiment is more realistic but still under-specified and limited. Important reproducibility details are missing or vague, including exact preprocessing choices, SGD/logistic regression hyperparameters, random seeds, calibration-bin handling, and full numerical tables. The paper reports small PPV/FOR gaps and accuracy loss, but does not provide enough diagnostics on calibration error or variance to establish robustness beyond the shown case.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the current manuscript. The paper states 'Code will be made available at' but leaves the location blank. Algorithm 1 is partly schematic, using an abstract 'Evaluate F' step, and several essential implementation details are pushed to appendices without a complete executable specification.

The presentation is mathematically dense and sometimes obscures the main contribution. Many derivations are long algebraic manipulations, while higher-level explanation of what is new relative to Baumann et al. and Zeng et al. is comparatively thin. The practical meaning of randomized decisions in high-stakes settings is also not discussed deeply enough.

The ethics/impact discussion is too cursory. The method explicitly uses protected attributes and may randomize decisions in domains such as lending, admissions, and criminal justice, but the paper does not adequately discuss legal, procedural, or stakeholder implications of randomized group-aware decision rules.

Overall, the theory has merit, but the paper does not yet provide sufficient empirical validation, reproducibility, or practical/ethical treatment for acceptance at the main ICML track. I would lean weak reject rather than outright reject because the geometric formulation is useful and potentially publishable after stronger positioning and evaluation.

strengths: The paper addresses a precise and important gap in fairness post-processing: exact optimal binary classification under sufficiency/predictive parity for finite-valued group-calibrated scores, a setting that is practically relevant for binned risk scores and not covered by prior continuous-support analyses.

The main technical contribution is strong: the feasible PPV/FOR region is characterized geometrically, the boundary is derived via a fractional-knapsack/soft-threshold argument, and the intersection of group-wise feasible regions yields an exact algorithm for optimizing losses and deviation from separation.

The presentation is generally clear for a theory-heavy paper. The figures help explain the feasible regions and why deterministic thresholds are often insufficient, and the appendices provide detailed derivations for the boundary, active-boundary checks, loss minimization, and separation-deviation objective.

The empirical section is appropriate for illustrating the theory: FICO and COMPAS show behavior on classic finite-score fairness settings, while ACS Income demonstrates an end-to-end pipeline with learned and calibrated scores. The reported accuracy losses are small while PPV/FOR gaps are substantially reduced.

The paper treats important limitations honestly, especially the reliance on group-calibrated scores, the finite-score assumption, binary protected groups in the main exposition, possible infeasibility with more groups, and the effect of approximate calibration. The calibration-error robustness appendix is a useful addition.

Reproducibility is reasonably good: algorithms are specified in detail, datasets and preprocessing are described, and most experiments use public data. The claim that code will be made available further supports reproducibility if fulfilled.
weaknesses: The central guarantees depend heavily on exact group calibration and known score-bin distributions. In realistic finite-sample settings these are estimated, and while the paper gives a calibration-error bound, the main optimality claims can be fragile when calibration or bin weights are noisy.

The empirical evaluation is mostly illustrative rather than deeply validating. Only three case studies are used, two rely on aggregate or manually constructed score models, and there is limited comparison against alternative post-processing methods beyond unconstrained thresholding.

The COMPAS experiment treats pooled empirical decile rates as group-calibrated despite acknowledging this is only approximate. This is acceptable as illustration, but it weakens any substantive fairness conclusion from that case study.

The method may require randomized decisions and explicit use of protected group membership at decision time. These are important deployment and policy issues; the impact statement is brief and could discuss these ethical and legal tradeoffs more concretely.

The paper states that the extension beyond binary protected groups is straightforward, but the main algorithm and exposition focus on two groups. More detail on computational scaling, feasibility, and behavior for many intersecting groups would strengthen the contribution.

The code availability statement appears incomplete/placeheld in the manuscript, and exact implementation details such as numerical stability around boundary roots and degenerate intersections are mostly left to appendices rather than demonstrated in released artifacts.
